targets.description: An acoustic rock kick drum (24-inch, hit hard, close and overhead mics): a round low thump with a short felt-beater click, a little room, decaying in under a second.
A classic 808-style electronic kick: a deep, clean sine boom with a fast pitch drop at the start and a short, smooth decay (about half a second). Mono.
An acoustic 14-inch snare drum hit hard: a crisp stick crack, a bright rattle of snare wires and a short body ring, with a little room around it; under a second.
A group handclap: several people clapping at once, a dense, slightly smeared crack with a very short room tail (about 0.3 s).
A closed hi-hat (14-inch) played with a stick: a tight, bright metallic tick with a short noisy sizzle, half a second at most.
An open hi-hat (14-inch): a bright, washy metallic sizzle that rings out for about a second and a half.
A 17-inch crash cymbal hit hard: an explosive, bright, wide metallic wash that decays slowly over several seconds.
An 18-inch floor tom hit hard with a stick: a deep, pitched boom with a stick attack and a ringing low body that decays over about 1.5 seconds.
A huge 22-inch tom hit hard with felt mallets, taiko-like: a massive, soft-edged low boom with lots of weight and a resonant decay of about 2 seconds.
An orchestral concert bass drum struck very hard: a vast, deep, rumbling boom in a hall, felt more than heard, with a long decay of several seconds.
An orchestral timpani hit fortissimo on a low note: a pitched, booming kettle drum with a soft mallet attack and a long resonant ring.
A low conga (tumba) open tone played by hand: a warm, rounded, pitched drum hit with a skin slap and a short ring (under a second).
A tambourine struck once: a bright, jangly shimmer of small metal jingles with a light skin tap, decaying in under a second.
A cinematic trailer boom: a huge, deep, distorted low-end explosion that blooms in over a fraction of a second and rumbles out over a few seconds. Mono.
A big cinematic impact: a heavy low boom with a metallic, reverberant hit layer on top, designed for trailers, with a long tail of several seconds. Mono.
A low-frequency explosion for a sci-fi game: a soft, sub-heavy whump that swells in quickly and fades out over about 2 seconds, with little top end. Mono.
A cinematic braam: a very low, buzzing, rasping brass blast (a trombone growl around A2) that swells in over half a second and holds briefly before stopping.
A cymbal swell used as a riser: a soft mallet roll on a suspended cymbal that builds from silence into a bright, loud metallic roar over about 4 seconds, then cuts off.
A short rising rumble: dark, windy low-frequency noise that grows louder over about 2 seconds and then drops away. Mono.
A downlifter: a bright, airy noise sweep that falls from very high to low over about 4 seconds, fading as it descends, wide stereo.
A slow, dark cinematic whoosh: a low, airy noise swell that rises over about a second, passes and fades out over the next two and a half.
A metal impact: a hammer striking an anvil, a hard, bright clang with high, inharmonic ringing partials that decays over about a second.
A concert harp plucked at C5: a clear, round, bell-like pluck with a soft attack and a warm ringing decay of a few seconds.
A kalimba (thumb piano) note around A5: a bright, woody, bell-like pluck with a little buzz, decaying over about two seconds.
A violin section playing pizzicato at C5: a short, soft, plucked string ensemble note with a little room ambience, about half a second.
A solo double bass plucked pizzicato on a low E (about 82 Hz): a round, woody, deep pluck with a thumpy attack and a ringing decay of about 2 seconds.
A thick synth bass note on C2 (about 65 Hz): a sustained, fat, buzzy analog-style tone whose filter moves slowly, held for 2 seconds. Mono.
A warm, evolving synth pad around G2: a soft, wide, slightly detuned and grainy chord texture that fades in gently and sustains.
A choir 'aah' pad: a soft, airy, high vocal ensemble tone that swells in and fades out over about a second and a half, wide stereo.
A tenor saxophone playing a sustained D5 without vibrato: a reedy, breathy, bright tone with a soft tongued attack, held for 3 seconds.
An upright piano playing A4 at medium-loud: a woody hammered attack with a bright, slightly honky tone that rings and decays over several seconds.
An FM electric piano (Yamaha TX81Z) playing C4: a glassy, bell-like tine attack with a mellow sustained tone that decays over about 3 seconds. Mono.
An orchestral tubular bell (chime) on C4 struck hard: a bright, clangorous metallic strike with inharmonic partials and a long shimmering ring of several seconds.
A marimba note on G5 struck loud: a warm, woody mallet hit with a short, round resonant decay of about a second.
A vibraphone note on A5 with hard mallets: a pure, bell-like metallic tone with a soft attack and a long, smooth ring of several seconds.
A trumpet staccato stab on D5, played loud: a short, bright, brassy blast with a crisp tongued attack and a quick release in a room.
A violin section spiccato stab at C5: a short, bouncy, bowed string ensemble note with a little bow noise, well under a second.
A cello section holding a D3 with vibrato: a warm, rich, bowed ensemble tone with a gentle attack, sustaining for 4 seconds.
A flute holding A5 with expressive vibrato: a pure, breathy, airy tone that swells in slowly and sustains.
Rain falling on a garage roof and gutter: a steady, dense, crackling texture of drops, mostly mid and high frequencies. Mono.
Outdoor wind: a broadband gusting noise that swells and eases, with low rumble and airy hiss. Mono.
Vinyl record surface noise: a constant soft hiss with scattered crackles and pops, in stereo.
A dark ambient drone around C3: a sustained, slowly shifting tonal hum with a hazy, wide texture.
A wine glass rubbed on the rim: a pure, singing, very sustained high tone (around 950 Hz) with a slow swell and a slight beating shimmer.
A short UI click: a tiny, dry, crisp tick for a button press, about 0.1 s. Mono.
A short electronic pop: a round, bubbly, synthetic blip under 0.1 s. Mono.
A short transition swoosh: a quick airy noise swipe that rises and falls in under a second. Mono.
A UI confirmation chime: a short, clean, pleasant electronic tone about a third of a second long. Mono.
A small sci-fi laser zap: a quick descending electronic pew with a buzzy tone, about a quarter of a second. Mono.
A vinyl record scratch: a DJ pushing the record back and forth, a short zippy, pitched noise gesture. Mono.
A crow caw: a single harsh, raspy bird call, about half a second. Mono.
A coin (a US quarter) dropped on a desk: a bright metallic ting and a short, tinkling rattle as it settles, half a second. Mono.
A flexatone shaken: a wobbly, warbling, bright metallic tone that swoops in pitch like a cartoon, with rapid beater rattles, a few seconds long.

A trance supersaw lead holding one note (A4): seven detuned sawtooth voices beating against each other, spread wide across the stereo field, bright, with a highpass keeping it clear of the bass; a quick attack, held about 2 s, then a short release.

A reese bass on one long low note (C2): detuned sawtooth-like voices whose phase slowly drifts, so a comb of notches sweeps up and down through the upper harmonics about every 3 s, giving a vowel-like, hollow movement; the fundamental is weak, the low end stays mono while the mids and highs are wide; 6 s, no attack or release to speak of.

An 808 bass: a clean sine boom on F1 with a fast pitch drop at the strike and soft saturation, then at about 0.6 s it glides up a fourth to A#1 and rings on with a long, slowly fading sub tail; about 3 s. Mono.

A short house pluck on C4: two slightly detuned sawtooth voices and a quiet square an octave down, through a resonant lowpass whose cutoff snaps from bright to dull within about 100 ms; the note dies away in under a second. Slightly wide.

A slowly moving synth pad: a soft, wide C major 9 chord (C3 up to D4) of pulse waves whose widths drift independently, through a lowpass that opens from dark to bright over about 2.3 s and closes again; slow attack of nearly a second, about 5 s with its release.

A dubstep wobble bass on F1: a saw and square through a driven resonant lowpass whose cutoff swings with a sine LFO at eighth notes of 140 BPM (about 4.7 wobbles a second), over a steady clean sine sub; 2 s. Mono.

An electronic chime: a metallic, inharmonic strike with partials spread from about 1.7 kHz to 8 kHz like an FM or ring-modulated bell, the brightest ones dying first so the tone darkens and thins over about 2 s; a hard, slightly clipped attack. Mono.

One TB-303 style acid bass note with accent and slide: an accented C2 sawtooth through a squelchy, highly resonant lowpass whose envelope sweeps down from bright, then a 60 ms slide up to G2 at 0.3 s; released at 0.75 s, about 1 s in all. Mono.

A rave hoover lead on C3: a thick, buzzy stack of pulse waves an octave apart with fast pulse-width movement and detune, diving down into the note from about a fifth above at the start, chorused wide, and falling an octave over the last half second; 2.5 s.
A detuned synth chord stab: a bright minor-seventh chord around G4 (G, B flat, D, F) with a fast attack and a decay of about a second, wide in stereo with a mono low end.

A growl bass: a two-operator FM tone on F2 whose brightness pulses about twice a second, through a formant filter swinging between "o" and "a" vowels, saturated, over a clean sine sub an octave down; 1.6 s. Mono.

A synth riser over 4 s: filtered white noise sweeping up from a low hiss to a bright 9 kHz band, plus three detuned saws gliding up two octaves from C3 as their lowpass opens; it swells from very quiet to full, widens in stereo as it rises, and stops dead at the top.
